Reading a Migration

Plain SQL, generated for you — worth reading once, never worth hand-editing.

The file Prisma generated is ordinary SQL — nothing Prisma-specific about it at all. Figure 2.10 is an excerpt of it.

-- Figure 2.10: a generated migration (prisma/migrations/20260909122353_init/migration.sql, excerpt)
CREATE TABLE `User` (
    `id` INTEGER NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
    `email` VARCHAR(191) NOT NULL,
    `role` ENUM('customer', 'agent', 'admin') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'customer',

    UNIQUE INDEX `User_email_key`(`email`),
    PRIMARY KEY (`id`)
);

-- AddForeignKey
ALTER TABLE `Ticket` ADD CONSTRAINT `Ticket_customerId_fkey`
  FOREIGN KEY (`customerId`) REFERENCES `User`(`id`)
  ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE;

Every piece traces straight back to schema.prisma: @id became PRIMARY KEY, @unique became a UNIQUE INDEX, the Role enum became MySQL's own ENUM type, and the customer relation from the one-to-many topic became an actual ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT foreign key — this is the point where a relation field you wrote in the schema turns into a real constraint the database itself will enforce.

The full file has one CREATE TABLE per model and one ALTER TABLE per relation, in the order Prisma needs to run them (tables before the foreign keys that reference them). You'll read files like this often, to see exactly what a schema change actually did to the database — but you never hand-edit one. Once a migration's been applied, it's a historical record; the way to change the schema further is always to edit schema.prisma again and run migrate dev again, which generates the next migration file rather than touching this one.
